Nowadays, it feels like most shows on basic television and streaming services are either whodunnits, grisly crime thrillers, or "eat the rich" satires . With A Murder at the End of the World , you get all three rolled into one. Despite receiving positive reviews upon release on FX/Hulu in 2023, the seven-episode miniseries, created by the duo of Brit Marling and Zal Batmanglij , seems to have been lost to time. With the cold weather upon us, there is no better time to catch up on this intense psychological thriller set on an isolated Arctic retreat in Iceland. Starring Emma Corrin , Harris Dickinson , Joan Chen , and Clive Owen , A Murder at the End of the World will keep you spooked and guessing. \'The OA\' Meets a Police Procedural in FX\'s \'A Murder at the End of the World\' Emma Corrin in the Murder at the End of the World finale Image via FX Brit Marling and Zal Batmanglij proved themselves to be a dynamic creative pair as co-creators of The OA , the two-season Netflix mystery drama starring Marling as the central character. Marling also starred and co-wrote the 2013 film, The East , a psychological drama directed by Batmanglij. The two clearly have chemistry, and their creative partnership culminated in their most enduring and fascinating work to date, A Murder at the End of the World , which ran from November 14 to December 19 in 2023. The series follows Darby Hart (Corrin), an amateur detective, and 8 other guests invited to a retreat at the secluded home of reclusive billionaire Andy Ronson (Owen), who was interested in Darby\'s publications as an independent sleuth. When one of the guests, Darby\'s former partner, Bill (Dickinson), is found dead, she must step up and become a sleuth on the spot to uncover the truth behind this bizarre mystery . The concept of strangers convening at a mysterious house only to encounter a murder with a perpetrator hiding in plain sight is nothing new, going all the way back to Agatha Christie novels and Clue , and most recently seen in Glass Onion: A Knives Out Mystery and Blink Twice . Amid contemporary economic distress and class alienation in everyday life, scathing critiques of the wealthy upper class have remained fresh in film and television, even if they have developed shorthand clichés. The FX/Hulu series expands upon the eerie depiction of the privileged class by also tackling other pressing societal anxieties , notably the dread of artificial intelligence and the general distortion of reality and fiction. Ronson, a tech tycoon sharing many traits with some of our most influential business leaders today, pretends to be an ally of Gen-Z dialogue and concerns, but the divide between him and Darby couldn\'t be further. \'A Murder at the End of the World\' Is a Sharp Murder Mystery Perfect for Gen Z Darby\'s status as a detective of Generation Z is the backbone of A Murder at the End of the World , as her trepidatious disposition and skepticism toward trusted institutions are emblematic of the disaffected nature of America\'s future. Being raised by a single father, as her mother left when she was a child, Darby had naturally been drawn to the dark underbelly of the world, and she spent most of her time browsing Reddit and its eerie wormholes. As a detective in a position of power to solve a cryptic mystery, Darby empowers the cynical worldview of the generation by channeling it into something impactful. This sincere dissection of values, characterized by Darby\'s determination to solve assault cases against women, often supplants the plot development of the murder mystery, but Marling and Batmanglij were far more intrigued by the mindset of a young detective. The series delivers as a procedural drama , filled with many gripping sequences of old-school detective work with a glossy technological spin and a provocative twist ending , so its commentary never hinders the viewing experience. If anything, the show is grounded compared to Marling and Batmanglij\'s abstract tendencies seen in The OA . Emma Corrin and Harris Dickinson Raise the Dramatic Stakes of \'A Murder at the End of the World\' Emma Corrin and Harris Dickinson in A Murder at the End of the World Image via FX Although Harris Dickinson, one of Hollywood\'s brightest stars, who is tapped to play John Lennon in Sam Mendes \' four-part Beatles biopic, is written out of the main narrative early, we see him interact with The Crown \'s Emma Corrin via flashbacks. Set six years prior to the events in the series, the flashbacks follow Darby and Bill as they uncover the remains of a victim of a suspected serial killer in the basement. While Darby is intoxicated by the case, even getting her father, a coroner, involved, Bill is cautious of her intrepid sleuthing, as he is grappling with the psychological ramifications of witnessing such carnage. As compelling as the present-day murder mystery is, A Murder at the End of the World is at its most dramatically immersive during these flashbacks , which underlines Darby\'s obsessive desires as a detective and the alienating effects these tendencies have on those surrounding her. Posts By Jessica Toomer Oct 26, 2025 From the get-go, thanks to the chilly, moody atmosphere, exceptionally deployed by the visual team, audiences suspect something is afoot in A Murder at the End of the World , and this overriding sense of dread hangs over the entire narrative. Fear lingers throughout each episode — fear of the future and the sinister truth of the murder mystery. "I didn’t know how to give up or how to sense danger when danger was closing in," Darby says to the audience, reflecting the toxic nature of her obsessive proclivities and egoism as a savior on the Internet. This concept comes alive in the various flashbacks between Darby and Bill, a running narrative that could\'ve served as its own stirring drama. IFC Films has debuted the full official trailer for 100 Nights of Hero , a fantasy romance thriller from the filmmaker Julia Jackman as her second film so far (after Bonus Track ). If the first trailer for Julia Jackman\'s starry Isabel Greenberg adaptation 100 Nights Of Hero is anything to go by though, then that archaic narrative is about to get one hell of a reframing. For Emma Corrin, Maika Monroe, Charli XCX, Nicholas Galitzine, and more ripping up the period piece rulebook in riotous fashion, check out the teaser below; Is 100 Nights Of Hero a feminist fairytale? An anti-misogynist manifesto? A fantastical fever dream loaded with sapphic tension, satirical swipes, and a surprise, blink-and-you\'ll-miss-it tease of a platinum-haired Felicity Jones? The answer, at least on present evidence, seems to very much be all of the above, and much more besides. Rather than a doomed bride telling her tormentor tall tales to curry favour, Jackman\'s movie — like Greenberg\'s graphic novel before it — looks to see Corrin\'s maid Hero regaling young bride Cherry (Monroe) with tales of rebellious women night after night to inspire in her the courage to basically tell future He-Man Nicholas Galitzine\'s darkly charismatic would-be suitor Manfred to do one. And it\'s going to do so with oodles of style, as the gorgeous costumes and quasi-Medieval setting — giving hints of Saltburn , Spencer , and even subtle notes of Francis Ford Coppola\'s decidedly unsubtle Bram Stoker\'s Dracula — attest. The short but sweet official synopsis for the movie reads as follows: "When her neglectful husband departs after placing a secret wager to test her fidelity, Cherry (Monroe) and her sharp-witted maid, Hero (Corrin), must fend off a dangerously seductive visitor: Manfred (Galitzine)." We\'ll find out if Cherry\'s holding out for a Hero pays off when 100 Nights Of Hero hits cinemas stateside on 5 December, and UK/Ireland multiplexes in early 2026. Corendon Airlines has launched a limited-time “Buy One Flight, Get One Free” deal on selected 2026 routes for Black Friday. The offer runs from 00:00 on 24 November until 23:59 on November 30, allowing travellers to snap up free second flights (up to two per passenger) on departures between April and 25 June 2026. The promotion comes as Turkey continues to attract British holidaymakers in record numbers, with celebrities such as Jason Statham, Emma Corrin and Anya Taylor-Joy choosing the country for their own getaways. Stansted Airport is set to play a central role in Corendon’s expanded operations for summer 2026. The airline will increase its daily flights to Antalya from the Essex hub, alongside additional frequencies from Gatwick, Birmingham, Glasgow, Manchester and Newcastle. The growth comes in response to Antalya Airport’s major expansion, which has boosted its capacity from 35 million to 82 million passengers. Crete will also see a lift, with Corendon increasing UK flights to Heraklion by 20%. A sample fare highlights the value of the Black Friday promotion: a one-way Eco flight from London Stansted to Antalya on 7 June 2026 would cost just £164* for two passengers under the “buy one, get one free” offer. Corendon Airlines, headquartered in Antalya, operates alongside sister carriers Corendon Dutch in Amsterdam and Corendon Europe in Malta. By Christian Zilko Plus icon Christian Zilko More stories by Christian ‘Carol & Joy’ Trailer: Carol Kane and Her 98-Year-Old Mother Share New York Stories Read more Will Arnett Thought He’d Never Land a Dramatic Role: ‘Why Would They?’ Read more ‘The Moment’ Teaser: Charli XCX Stars in A24 Music Industry Satire Inspired by Her Own Idea Read more November 3, 2025 2:18 pm \'100 Nights of Hero\' Courtesy of IFC Films Share Share on Facebook Post google Google Preferred Share on LinkedIn Show more sharing options Share to Flipboard Submit to Reddit Pin it Post to Tumblr Email Print This Page Share on WhatsApp The classic narrative structure of “One Thousand and One Nights,” which saw a woman who marries a prince with a penchant for killing his brides extend her own life via a series of riveting stories, gets a modern feminist update this holiday season in the form of Julia Jackman’s “100 Nights of Hero.” Adapted from Isabel Greenberg’s 2016 graphic novel, the film follows a maid who attempts to protect a young bride from a dreadful fate by telling her a series of stories. Emma Corrin stars as the titular storyteller alongside Maika Monroe, with Nicholas Galitzine, Amir El-Masry, Charli XCX , Richard E. Grant, and Felicity Jones rounding out the rest of the supporting cast. Related Stories The Hard Choices Public Media Institutions Are Facing Every Single Day Two Weeks on ‘Eyes Wide Shut’ Turned Into Four Years: Shooting Second Unit for Stanley Kubrick “ 100 Nights of Hero ” premiered at the 2025 Venice International Film Festival , where it earned overwhelming praise for its sharp pop sensibilities and writer/director Julia Jackman’s ability to update a classic storytelling format for more contemporary sensibilities. “What makes the work remarkable is its sincerity,” Leila Latif wrote in her IndieWire review. “In a cinematic landscape increasingly dominated by algorithm-driven sameness, this film stands out for its defiant originality. It revels in its singularity and empathy, in the radical power of storytelling: to distract tyrants, to empower the silenced, to imagine new futures. The act of telling a story becomes, in itself, an act of survival and resistance. That message, articulated through Cherry and Hero’s connection, resonates far beyond the screen. By the end, one feels not just entertained, but invigorated. Jackman’s film is a joyous testament to independence, creativity, and the enduring necessity of stories. It proves that happy endings need not conform to centuries-old formulas, and that love, be it romantic, platonic, queer, or fleeting, can be as complex and wondrous as any of the tales we tell.” She continued, “This is a film of rare joy and spirit, and one that deserves to be celebrated as both a feminist fairytale and a manifesto that will inspire a myriad of future stories.” An Independent Film Company release, “100 Nights of Hero” opens in theaters on Friday, December 5. An Independent Film Company Release.) Queer writer/director Julia Jackman (“Bonus Track”) has crafted a stylish and clever queer romance with “100 Nights of Hero,” opening in area theatres Dec. 5. The film, adapted from Isabel Greenberg’s graphic novel, “The One Hundred Nights of Hero,” is set in a fictional medieval land where a woman’s place is to marry and have sons, not to read or write. This arch film recounts the story of Cherry (Maika Monroe), who is pressured to have a son with her husband, Jerome (Amir El-Masry). Alas, Jerome “prefers to hunt and ride, and play darts with his handsome friends rather than spend time in the bedroom with his wife.” Enter Manfred (Nicholas Galitzine), a rake who bets Jerome that he can seduce Cherry, whom Jerome insists is a “paragon of virtue.” One obstacle to Manfred’s plan is Cherry’s handmaiden, Hero (Emma Corrin), who is happy to distract Manfred by telling stories. The story-within-the-film is a feminist tale about Rosa (Charli XCX) resisting a marriage. “100 Nights of Hero,” has great fun as Hero teaches Cherry how to kiss and Manfred tries to weasel his way into Cherry’s bedroom. The costumes and set design are fabulous and the cast delivers the witty dialogue with aplomb. Jackman spoke with PGN about making her fabulous fairytale. The film is about women telling stories to save themselves and start a revolution. What can you say about (re)telling the stories in “100 Nights of Hero”? Creating this impression of a population that has been waiting for a spark for a long time is a challenge. I loved this idea of Isabel taking inspiration from “One Thousand and One Nights” and making this graphic novel, and I took inspiration from that and made a film. There is a progression of stories of women talking to each other and essentially comparing notes. The thread for me was how crucial it is to keep communicating with each other in a world that doesn’t necessarily want people to be sharing or controlling information. What approach did you take to adapting the beloved graphic novel? Preserving the heart of the graphic novel — its playfulness and its revolutionary heart — was really important to me. The novel was quite anthological. I ended up fleshing out much of the main storyline. You spend less time with Cherry and Hero and Manfred in the graphic novel. They are fixed in their roles; Cherry and Hero are already a secret couple and Manfred is an old, dastardly villain. In the spirit of Isabel’s sense of camp, I leaned into this fluidity, and how much society tries to impose these structures. The most macho men have an air of homoeroticism and attraction between them. Cherry and Hero’s love story and intimacy was incredibly important, but I wanted to start them in that classic queer coming-of-age state, where you have this best friend you think is incredible and beautiful, and you want to spend all your time with them but you don’t recognize that feeling as being in love until later — especially in a world that tells you that it is wrong, or forbidden. But the forbidden-ness can make it more exciting and scary. This queer forbidden love has intimacy first that builds to attraction and queer yearning and the feeling of not even allowing yourself to want something because you are so sure you can’t have it. That was where I wanted them to start — in love and in denial as opposed to fully together. The film is both a fairytale and a feminist fable. What decisions did you make with creating the tone of the film? That was something that is different on screen. It was present in the graphic novel. Isabel had this playfulness and wit to her writing that was often quite deadpan, so by the time the sincerity and emotion and anger came in, you felt that it snuck up on you in this way. It has always been a tricky tone — as in challenging, as in tricksy, where what you think you are watching changes throughout. I leaned into that and the idea that Hero — if the story itself is about this underestimated person lulling people into a scenario by appealing to what they think it’s going to be — that the film takes that direction itself. Isabel’s graphic novel has that meta element, but it was definitely pumped up in the film. You have this feeling it’s going to be this really steamy love triangle. Manfred thinks he’s going to seduce this woman and keep a castle and he’s just listening to another woman talking. There is that slipperiness intrinsic in the scheme as well. Emma Corrin and Maika Monroe in Julia Jackman’s ‘100 Nights of Hero.’ (Photo: Courtesy of Independent Film Company. An Independent Film Company Release) The film has a distinctive look, with amazing costumes, set design and imagery. Can you talk about world-building? Obviously, massive kudos to Susie Coulthard and Sofia Sacomani, our costumes and production designer, respectively, and to Paul Rice, our visual effects supervisor who created the stained glass and the moons. The costumes were custom-made by Susie and her team. I had a mood board, and my main inspiration were the silly hats. Which were camp and pointed to this idea of the theatricality of roles people are expected to play in society. But I wanted it to feel a little more out of time and more gothic than the graphic novel. It was interesting to see what was possible. There is a very queer bent here, with Jerome being clocked as queer, and Hero teaching Cherry how to kiss. What can you say about playing the queer content up or down? It is both overt and subversive. A litmus test for me is that I can tell who laughs when Cherry and Hero say they are “best friends.” I feel the gays intrinsically understand that right away. Some take it at face value. The graphic novel doesn’t have any sex in it at all. I respected the yearning quality of it, but I did want to pump it up a little bit. It felt to me, especially as with a lot of lesbian stories, there is this idea there is going to be a lot of hand brushing and then suddenly people are furiously scissoring. It wasn’t about shame or what the characters themselves felt, but it was in a world without freedom, and I wanted to pump up the horniness while honoring the fact that this is a story of people who were never taught to act on their desires and the stakes were high if they did. In the end, I shot one full sex scene, and I put it in the sky in the end with this idea: Is it a flashback, or what they would do if they were together? The film is about women fighting the patriarchy and the rules of society, to become educated and empowered. Cherry is supposed to get married, have children, do needlepoint and then die. Knowing Hero and hearing her stories makes her wish she lived a braver life. Why do you think this message still resonates today? I hope that it would say to people that the powers that be are going to push people who historically have been on the margins back into the margins. I hope it shows that when we keep talking, and have each other’s backs, and keep insisting on having a seat at the table — whether it is what we are allowed to know, allowed to see, or the public spaces we are allowed to inhabit — you don’t give that up, that we keep talking to each other. People are going to try to make you feel like you are alone and ashamed and you’re not. The biggest tool they have is if people are isolated from each other. It’s a rallying call against that shame and self-isolation. Arkasha Stevenson and Tim Smith have been working on an untitled project for A24 and a star-studded cast is being assembled, with Havana Rose Liu and Sophie Wilde also set to join. I’m grateful, obviously, for everything my work brings my way, but as you get older and you think about what you want for the rest of your life… I’m trying to find a balance of liking the work I’m doing and the choices I’m making, and distancing myself from [the rest]... Focus Features Culture Books Why More Men Should Read Jane Austen Why More Men Should Read Jane Austen Not just the lady on your £10 note By Henry Wong Published: 04 November 2025 We are nearing the end of 2025, which I am sure you know marks 250 years since the birth of Jane Austen (she’s older than America, which turned a sprightly 249 in July). Perhaps you know this because you keep a spreadsheet of significant cultural anniversaries (just us?) or maybe you were alerted by the slew of new Austen adaptations coming soon to screens near you ( Sense and Sensibility with Daisy Edgar-Jones; Pride and Prejudice with Emma Corrin). Or you could be one of those people who pay attention to book sales and noted that this year marked a 15-year high for Austen’s titles (thank you limited editions of things most of us already own). Well, I was aware of this semiquincentennial – a real term, I promise – because I live in the past and never knowingly venture into the 21 st century. I’m joking, of course. It is hard not to be alive in 2025 and know about everything going on. The news, the reaction to the news, the TikToks about the reaction to the news: a seductive, repulsive, endless drone. The only half-decent solution I’ve found – an actual route to feeling like a human being again – is to read books , and specifically fiction. It’s so boring to make this observation, as mundane as a parent telling their child that they should eat greens or not to talk to strangers or that the sky is blue because... well, actually I am not sure about that one. But yesterday, after a fortnight of too much drinking and not enough thinking, I plonked myself in a bath, read a few chapters of Persuasion and immediately felt about 300 times better. We cannot attribute that solely to the healing power of hot water, though no doubt the founder of your local sauna would sell you on that. What to Read Next Pride and Prejudice £7 at Amazon Reading Austen is a little like how I imagine some people feel about AI: totally thrilling, a little disorientating, a new world of possibility despite the Regency furnishings. She is funny, and smart, and mean, and compassionate, and capable of conveying about seventeen emotions in a single chapter. Austen was in her early 20s when she wrote most of her six era-defining books, a fact which will both inspire and sicken you depending on your age and literary ambitions. She died, from illness, at the age of 41. What did the world lose with that untimely death? Who knows. Let us focus on what we gained. Persuasion £7 at Amazon Not to sound like your creative writing teacher – and feel free to skip ahead if you flunked GCSE English – but Austen was a pioneer of free indirect discourse, which sounds like a description of trading routes but is actually just a fun way to tell a story. Austen simply slips a character’s thoughts into the third-person narrative, meaning readers are fully enveloped in these people’s minds. It’s why you remember Caroline Bingley’s snobbery about the Bennetts in Pride and Prejudice. And Emma Woodhouse’s silly, bitter, wonderful voice – Austen’s most awe-inspiring creation – throughout Emma . When you read Persuasion , and you are compelled by all of Anne Elliot’s life choices, you can thank Austen’s literary innovation. Henry James, Virginia Woolf, James Joyce would follow suit, and it is difficult to picture contemporary fiction without Austen’s influence. Certainly, we would not have nearly as many Austen adaptations – from Dakota Johnson’s underrated take on Persuasion to Autumn de Wilde’s Emma. and countless BBC series – if it were not for the author’s piercing writing style. I can’t help but thinking of Austen when we talk about the problems that currently plague our culture (and not least because I yearn for a writer with her talents to take on such anxieties). About our rapidly dwindling attention spans and second-screening habits. How our time-engulfing algorithms feed us content, which is at best nonsensical and at worse dangerous. And specially, how men are susceptible to such traps, both falling prey to and taking part in harmful narratives and conspiracies. Enter Austen, who knew better than most how to make us feel for unlikeable and intriguing characters, often hemmed in by their sex or circumstance. And she knew how to do it with jokes. Northanger Abbey £4 at Amazon I am not Polyannaish enough to suggest that reading would solve all these problems – and many well-read people have inflicted harm on this world – though it is hard to think of a more immediate and accessible way to improve people’s empathy than inhabiting the lives of other people for a few hundred pages . At the very least, it would reduce our screen time. (By the way, Austen was born on 16 December, which gives you just over a month to get started in time for the precise anniversary of her birth. Start with Persuasion .) (Image credit: Universal) The First Omen director Arkasha Stevenson is putting together a stellar cast for her new horror movie for A24 , which has yet to confirm an official title. Per Variety , Five Nights at Freddy\'s star Josh Hutcherson, Fear the Walking Dead\'s Frank Dillane, Weapons star Whitmer Thomas, and Get Out\'s Caleb Landry Jones are all in talks to join the upcoming movie. The report arrived only a day after Emma Corrin, Hunter Schafer, Bottoms\' Havana Rose Liu, and Talk to Me star Sophie Wilde were confirmed to be the first members of the cast. Stevenson is reuniting with co-writer Tim Smith for this movie, which is set to follow "a bachelor party that spirals into terror". No further plot details have been revealed at this point, but the star-studded cast has instantly made the film one of the most exciting upcoming horror movies in cinemas. Stevenson debuted as director to wide critical acclaim with The First Omen, a prequel to the legendary horror saga. In GamesRadar+\'s four-star review , we called it "devilishly good" and "a smartly chilling \'70s-styled screamfest". It followed a young novice (played by Servant\'s Nell Tiger Free) who travels from the US to Italy to start a new life of religious servitude, but she is drawn into a dark conspiracy, uncovering terrifying truths. Now, the filmmaker is hoping to deliver another bone-chilling movie, working with some of the most popular stars working today, with Deadpool and Wolverine star Emma Corrin and Euphoria\'s Hunter Schafer leading the charge. Meanwhile, Josh Hutcherson is set to reprise his role in the upcoming Five Nights at Freddy’s 2 next month, while Whitmer Thomas has recently starred in one of the most talked-about horrors of the year, Zach Cregger\'s Weapons. Nowadays, it feels like most shows on basic television and streaming services are either whodunnits, grisly crime thrillers, or "eat the rich" satires . With A Murder at the End of the World , you get all three rolled into one. Despite receiving positive reviews upon release on FX/Hulu in 2023, the seven-episode miniseries, created by the duo of Brit Marling and Zal Batmanglij , seems to have been lost to time. With the cold weather upon us, there is no better time to catch up on this intense psychological thriller set on an isolated Arctic retreat in Iceland. Starring Emma Corrin , Harris Dickinson , Joan Chen , and Clive Owen , A Murder at the End of the World will keep you spooked and guessing. \'The OA\' Meets a Police Procedural in FX\'s \'A Murder at the End of the World\' Emma Corrin in the Murder at the End of the World finale Image via FX Brit Marling and Zal Batmanglij proved themselves to be a dynamic creative pair as co-creators of The OA , the two-season Netflix mystery drama starring Marling as the central character. Marling also starred and co-wrote the 2013 film, The East , a psychological drama directed by Batmanglij. The two clearly have chemistry, and their creative partnership culminated in their most enduring and fascinating work to date, A Murder at the End of the World , which ran from November 14 to December 19 in 2023. The series follows Darby Hart (Corrin), an amateur detective, and 8 other guests invited to a retreat at the secluded home of reclusive billionaire Andy Ronson (Owen), who was interested in Darby\'s publications as an independent sleuth. When one of the guests, Darby\'s former partner, Bill (Dickinson), is found dead, she must step up and become a sleuth on the spot to uncover the truth behind this bizarre mystery . The concept of strangers convening at a mysterious house only to encounter a murder with a perpetrator hiding in plain sight is nothing new, going all the way back to Agatha Christie novels and Clue , and most recently seen in Glass Onion: A Knives Out Mystery and Blink Twice . Amid contemporary economic distress and class alienation in everyday life, scathing critiques of the wealthy upper class have remained fresh in film and television, even if they have developed shorthand clichés. The FX/Hulu series expands upon the eerie depiction of the privileged class by also tackling other pressing societal anxieties , notably the dread of artificial intelligence and the general distortion of reality and fiction. Ronson, a tech tycoon sharing many traits with some of our most influential business leaders today, pretends to be an ally of Gen-Z dialogue and concerns, but the divide between him and Darby couldn\'t be further. \'A Murder at the End of the World\' Is a Sharp Murder Mystery Perfect for Gen Z Darby\'s status as a detective of Generation Z is the backbone of A Murder at the End of the World , as her trepidatious disposition and skepticism toward trusted institutions are emblematic of the disaffected nature of America\'s future. Being raised by a single father, as her mother left when she was a child, Darby had naturally been drawn to the dark underbelly of the world, and she spent most of her time browsing Reddit and its eerie wormholes. As a detective in a position of power to solve a cryptic mystery, Darby empowers the cynical worldview of the generation by channeling it into something impactful. This sincere dissection of values, characterized by Darby\'s determination to solve assault cases against women, often supplants the plot development of the murder mystery, but Marling and Batmanglij were far more intrigued by the mindset of a young detective. The series delivers as a procedural drama , filled with many gripping sequences of old-school detective work with a glossy technological spin and a provocative twist ending , so its commentary never hinders the viewing experience. If anything, the show is grounded compared to Marling and Batmanglij\'s abstract tendencies seen in The OA . Emma Corrin and Harris Dickinson Raise the Dramatic Stakes of \'A Murder at the End of the World\' Emma Corrin and Harris Dickinson in A Murder at the End of the World Image via FX Although Harris Dickinson, one of Hollywood\'s brightest stars, who is tapped to play John Lennon in Sam Mendes \' four-part Beatles biopic, is written out of the main narrative early, we see him interact with The Crown \'s Emma Corrin via flashbacks. Set six years prior to the events in the series, the flashbacks follow Darby and Bill as they uncover the remains of a victim of a suspected serial killer in the basement. While Darby is intoxicated by the case, even getting her father, a coroner, involved, Bill is cautious of her intrepid sleuthing, as he is grappling with the psychological ramifications of witnessing such carnage. As compelling as the present-day murder mystery is, A Murder at the End of the World is at its most dramatically immersive during these flashbacks , which underlines Darby\'s obsessive desires as a detective and the alienating effects these tendencies have on those surrounding her. Fear lingers throughout each episode — fear of the future and the sinister truth of the murder mystery. "I didn’t know how to give up or how to sense danger when danger was closing in," Darby says to the audience, reflecting the toxic nature of her obsessive proclivities and egoism as a savior on the Internet. This concept comes alive in the various flashbacks between Darby and Bill, a running narrative that could\'ve served as its own stirring drama. So, when Jerome mysteriously goes on a \'business trip\' and leaves Cherry with his flirtatious friend Manfred, Hero has a bad feeling. If the first trailer for Julia Jackman\'s starry Isabel Greenberg adaptation 100 Nights Of Hero is anything to go by though, then that archaic narrative is about to get one hell of a reframing. For Emma Corrin, Maika Monroe, Charli XCX, Nicholas Galitzine, and more ripping up the period piece rulebook in riotous fashion, check out the teaser below; Is 100 Nights Of Hero a feminist fairytale? The answer, at least on present evidence, seems to very much be all of the above, and much more besides. Rather than a doomed bride telling her tormentor tall tales to curry favour, Jackman\'s movie — like Greenberg\'s graphic novel before it — looks to see Corrin\'s maid Hero regaling young bride Cherry (Monroe) with tales of rebellious women night after night to inspire in her the courage to basically tell future He-Man Nicholas Galitzine\'s darkly charismatic would-be suitor Manfred to do one. And it\'s going to do so with oodles of style, as the gorgeous costumes and quasi-Medieval setting — giving hints of Saltburn , Spencer , and even subtle notes of Francis Ford Coppola\'s decidedly unsubtle Bram Stoker\'s Dracula — attest. The short but sweet official synopsis for the movie reads as follows: "When her neglectful husband departs after placing a secret wager to test her fidelity, Cherry (Monroe) and her sharp-witted maid, Hero (Corrin), must fend off a dangerously seductive visitor: Manfred (Galitzine)." We\'ll find out if Cherry\'s holding out for a Hero pays off when 100 Nights Of Hero hits cinemas stateside on 5 December, and UK/Ireland multiplexes in early 2026. TRAILER ‘100 Nights of Hero’ Trailer: Julia Jackman Crafts a Modern Fairy Tale with the Help of Charli XCX Emma Corrin and Maika Monroe star in Jackman\'s updated take on "One Thousand and One Nights," which earned rave reviews after its Venice premiere. By Christian Zilko Plus icon Christian Zilko More stories by Christian ‘Carol & Joy’ Trailer: Carol Kane and Her 98-Year-Old Mother Share New York Stories Read more Will Arnett Thought He’d Never Land a Dramatic Role: ‘Why Would They?’ Read more ‘The Moment’ Teaser: Charli XCX Stars in A24 Music Industry Satire Inspired by Her Own Idea Read more November 3, 2025 2:18 pm \'100 Nights of Hero\' Courtesy of IFC Films Share Share on Facebook Post google Google Preferred Share on LinkedIn Show more sharing options Share to Flipboard Submit to Reddit Pin it Post to Tumblr Email Print This Page Share on WhatsApp The classic narrative structure of “One Thousand and One Nights,” which saw a woman who marries a prince with a penchant for killing his brides extend her own life via a series of riveting stories, gets a modern feminist update this holiday season in the form of Julia Jackman’s “100 Nights of Hero.” Adapted from Isabel Greenberg’s 2016 graphic novel, the film follows a maid who attempts to protect a young bride from a dreadful fate by telling her a series of stories. Emma Corrin stars as the titular storyteller alongside Maika Monroe, with Nicholas Galitzine, Amir El-Masry, Charli XCX , Richard E. Grant, and Felicity Jones rounding out the rest of the supporting cast. Related Stories The Hard Choices Public Media Institutions Are Facing Every Single Day Two Weeks on ‘Eyes Wide Shut’ Turned Into Four Years: Shooting Second Unit for Stanley Kubrick “ 100 Nights of Hero ” premiered at the 2025 Venice International Film Festival , where it earned overwhelming praise for its sharp pop sensibilities and writer/director Julia Jackman’s ability to update a classic storytelling format for more contemporary sensibilities. “What makes the work remarkable is its sincerity,” Leila Latif wrote in her IndieWire review. “In a cinematic landscape increasingly dominated by algorithm-driven sameness, this film stands out for its defiant originality. It revels in its singularity and empathy, in the radical power of storytelling: to distract tyrants, to empower the silenced, to imagine new futures. The act of telling a story becomes, in itself, an act of survival and resistance. That message, articulated through Cherry and Hero’s connection, resonates far beyond the screen. By the end, one feels not just entertained, but invigorated. Jackman’s film is a joyous testament to independence, creativity, and the enduring necessity of stories. It proves that happy endings need not conform to centuries-old formulas, and that love, be it romantic, platonic, queer, or fleeting, can be as complex and wondrous as any of the tales we tell.” She continued, “This is a film of rare joy and spirit, and one that deserves to be celebrated as both a feminist fairytale and a manifesto that will inspire a myriad of future stories.” An Independent Film Company release, “100 Nights of Hero” opens in theaters on Friday, December 5. An Independent Film Company Release.) Queer writer/director Julia Jackman (“Bonus Track”) has crafted a stylish and clever queer romance with “100 Nights of Hero,” opening in area theatres Dec. 5. The film, adapted from Isabel Greenberg’s graphic novel, “The One Hundred Nights of Hero,” is set in a fictional medieval land where a woman’s place is to marry and have sons, not to read or write. This arch film recounts the story of Cherry (Maika Monroe), who is pressured to have a son with her husband, Jerome (Amir El-Masry). Alas, Jerome “prefers to hunt and ride, and play darts with his handsome friends rather than spend time in the bedroom with his wife.” Enter Manfred (Nicholas Galitzine), a rake who bets Jerome that he can seduce Cherry, whom Jerome insists is a “paragon of virtue.” One obstacle to Manfred’s plan is Cherry’s handmaiden, Hero (Emma Corrin), who is happy to distract Manfred by telling stories. The story-within-the-film is a feminist tale about Rosa (Charli XCX) resisting a marriage. “100 Nights of Hero,” has great fun as Hero teaches Cherry how to kiss and Manfred tries to weasel his way into Cherry’s bedroom. The costumes and set design are fabulous and the cast delivers the witty dialogue with aplomb. Jackman spoke with PGN about making her fabulous fairytale. The film is about women telling stories to save themselves and start a revolution. What can you say about (re)telling the stories in “100 Nights of Hero”? Creating this impression of a population that has been waiting for a spark for a long time is a challenge. I loved this idea of Isabel taking inspiration from “One Thousand and One Nights” and making this graphic novel, and I took inspiration from that and made a film. There is a progression of stories of women talking to each other and essentially comparing notes. The thread for me was how crucial it is to keep communicating with each other in a world that doesn’t necessarily want people to be sharing or controlling information. What approach did you take to adapting the beloved graphic novel? Preserving the heart of the graphic novel — its playfulness and its revolutionary heart — was really important to me. The novel was quite anthological. I ended up fleshing out much of the main storyline. You spend less time with Cherry and Hero and Manfred in the graphic novel. They are fixed in their roles; Cherry and Hero are already a secret couple and Manfred is an old, dastardly villain. In the spirit of Isabel’s sense of camp, I leaned into this fluidity, and how much society tries to impose these structures. The most macho men have an air of homoeroticism and attraction between them. Cherry and Hero’s love story and intimacy was incredibly important, but I wanted to start them in that classic queer coming-of-age state, where you have this best friend you think is incredible and beautiful, and you want to spend all your time with them but you don’t recognize that feeling as being in love until later — especially in a world that tells you that it is wrong, or forbidden. But the forbidden-ness can make it more exciting and scary. This queer forbidden love has intimacy first that builds to attraction and queer yearning and the feeling of not even allowing yourself to want something because you are so sure you can’t have it. That was where I wanted them to start — in love and in denial as opposed to fully together. The film is both a fairytale and a feminist fable. What decisions did you make with creating the tone of the film? That was something that is different on screen. It was present in the graphic novel. Isabel had this playfulness and wit to her writing that was often quite deadpan, so by the time the sincerity and emotion and anger came in, you felt that it snuck up on you in this way. It has always been a tricky tone — as in challenging, as in tricksy, where what you think you are watching changes throughout. I leaned into that and the idea that Hero — if the story itself is about this underestimated person lulling people into a scenario by appealing to what they think it’s going to be — that the film takes that direction itself. Isabel’s graphic novel has that meta element, but it was definitely pumped up in the film. You have this feeling it’s going to be this really steamy love triangle. Manfred thinks he’s going to seduce this woman and keep a castle and he’s just listening to another woman talking. There is that slipperiness intrinsic in the scheme as well. Emma Corrin and Maika Monroe in Julia Jackman’s ‘100 Nights of Hero.’ (Photo: Courtesy of Independent Film Company. An Independent Film Company Release) The film has a distinctive look, with amazing costumes, set design and imagery. Can you talk about world-building? Obviously, massive kudos to Susie Coulthard and Sofia Sacomani, our costumes and production designer, respectively, and to Paul Rice, our visual effects supervisor who created the stained glass and the moons. The costumes were custom-made by Susie and her team. I had a mood board, and my main inspiration were the silly hats. Which were camp and pointed to this idea of the theatricality of roles people are expected to play in society. But I wanted it to feel a little more out of time and more gothic than the graphic novel. It was interesting to see what was possible. There is a very queer bent here, with Jerome being clocked as queer, and Hero teaching Cherry how to kiss. What can you say about playing the queer content up or down? It is both overt and subversive. A litmus test for me is that I can tell who laughs when Cherry and Hero say they are “best friends.” I feel the gays intrinsically understand that right away. Some take it at face value. The graphic novel doesn’t have any sex in it at all. I respected the yearning quality of it, but I did want to pump it up a little bit. It felt to me, especially as with a lot of lesbian stories, there is this idea there is going to be a lot of hand brushing and then suddenly people are furiously scissoring. It wasn’t about shame or what the characters themselves felt, but it was in a world without freedom, and I wanted to pump up the horniness while honoring the fact that this is a story of people who were never taught to act on their desires and the stakes were high if they did. In the end, I shot one full sex scene, and I put it in the sky in the end with this idea: Is it a flashback, or what they would do if they were together? The film is about women fighting the patriarchy and the rules of society, to become educated and empowered. Cherry is supposed to get married, have children, do needlepoint and then die. Knowing Hero and hearing her stories makes her wish she lived a braver life. Why do you think this message still resonates today? I hope that it would say to people that the powers that be are going to push people who historically have been on the margins back into the margins. I hope it shows that when we keep talking, and have each other’s backs, and keep insisting on having a seat at the table — whether it is what we are allowed to know, allowed to see, or the public spaces we are allowed to inhabit — you don’t give that up, that we keep talking to each other. People are going to try to make you feel like you are alone and ashamed and you’re not. The biggest tool they have is if people are isolated from each other. It’s a rallying call against that shame and self-isolation. Arkasha Stevenson and Tim Smith have been working on an untitled project for A24 and a star-studded cast is being assembled, with Havana Rose Liu and Sophie Wilde also set to join. The 29-year-old star told Britain\'s ELLE magazine: "It’s a very weird aspect of this job. I find it really hard. I’m grateful, obviously, for everything my work brings my way, but as you get older and you think about what you want for the rest of your life… I’m trying to find a balance of liking the work I’m doing and the choices I’m making, and distancing myself from [the rest]... "I think playing Diana was, in a way, the greatest warning." Emma can next be seen in an episode of Black Mirror with Issa Rae which explores the advancement of AI in film, but in real life, the star is "terrified" by the use of technology in the arts. They said: "I’m not a fan. I think it’s terrible, actually. It terrifies me. "The loss of original, organic creativity and [not] having to be in a room with a group of people to create something is terrifying. "That’s the source of everything, isn’t it? The source of hope." Focus Features Culture Books Why More Men Should Read Jane Austen Why More Men Should Read Jane Austen Not just the lady on your £10 note By Henry Wong Published: 04 November 2025 We are nearing the end of 2025, which I am sure you know marks 250 years since the birth of Jane Austen (she’s older than America, which turned a sprightly 249 in July). Perhaps you know this because you keep a spreadsheet of significant cultural anniversaries (just us?) or maybe you were alerted by the slew of new Austen adaptations coming soon to screens near you ( Sense and Sensibility with Daisy Edgar-Jones; Pride and Prejudice with Emma Corrin). Or you could be one of those people who pay attention to book sales and noted that this year marked a 15-year high for Austen’s titles (thank you limited editions of things most of us already own). Well, I was aware of this semiquincentennial – a real term, I promise – because I live in the past and never knowingly venture into the 21 st century. I’m joking, of course. It is hard not to be alive in 2025 and know about everything going on. The news, the reaction to the news, the TikToks about the reaction to the news: a seductive, repulsive, endless drone. The only half-decent solution I’ve found – an actual route to feeling like a human being again – is to read books , and specifically fiction. It’s so boring to make this observation, as mundane as a parent telling their child that they should eat greens or not to talk to strangers or that the sky is blue because... well, actually I am not sure about that one. But yesterday, after a fortnight of too much drinking and not enough thinking, I plonked myself in a bath, read a few chapters of Persuasion and immediately felt about 300 times better. We cannot attribute that solely to the healing power of hot water, though no doubt the founder of your local sauna would sell you on that. What to Read Next Pride and Prejudice £7 at Amazon Reading Austen is a little like how I imagine some people feel about AI: totally thrilling, a little disorientating, a new world of possibility despite the Regency furnishings. She is funny, and smart, and mean, and compassionate, and capable of conveying about seventeen emotions in a single chapter. Austen was in her early 20s when she wrote most of her six era-defining books, a fact which will both inspire and sicken you depending on your age and literary ambitions. She died, from illness, at the age of 41. What did the world lose with that untimely death? Who knows. Let us focus on what we gained. Persuasion £7 at Amazon Not to sound like your creative writing teacher – and feel free to skip ahead if you flunked GCSE English – but Austen was a pioneer of free indirect discourse, which sounds like a description of trading routes but is actually just a fun way to tell a story. Austen simply slips a character’s thoughts into the third-person narrative, meaning readers are fully enveloped in these people’s minds. It’s why you remember Caroline Bingley’s snobbery about the Bennetts in Pride and Prejudice. And Emma Woodhouse’s silly, bitter, wonderful voice – Austen’s most awe-inspiring creation – throughout Emma . When you read Persuasion , and you are compelled by all of Anne Elliot’s life choices, you can thank Austen’s literary innovation. Henry James, Virginia Woolf, James Joyce would follow suit, and it is difficult to picture contemporary fiction without Austen’s influence. Certainly, we would not have nearly as many Austen adaptations – from Dakota Johnson’s underrated take on Persuasion to Autumn de Wilde’s Emma. and countless BBC series – if it were not for the author’s piercing writing style. I can’t help but thinking of Austen when we talk about the problems that currently plague our culture (and not least because I yearn for a writer with her talents to take on such anxieties). About our rapidly dwindling attention spans and second-screening habits. How our time-engulfing algorithms feed us content, which is at best nonsensical and at worse dangerous. And specially, how men are susceptible to such traps, both falling prey to and taking part in harmful narratives and conspiracies. Enter Austen, who knew better than most how to make us feel for unlikeable and intriguing characters, often hemmed in by their sex or circumstance. And she knew how to do it with jokes. Northanger Abbey £4 at Amazon I am not Polyannaish enough to suggest that reading would solve all these problems – and many well-read people have inflicted harm on this world – though it is hard to think of a more immediate and accessible way to improve people’s empathy than inhabiting the lives of other people for a few hundred pages . At the very least, it would reduce our screen time. (By the way, Austen was born on 16 December, which gives you just over a month to get started in time for the precise anniversary of her birth. Start with Persuasion .) Jordan and Juno Temple have joined the voice cast of Skydance Animation ’s upcoming animated feature Swapped , which is set to release in 2026. Swapped , formerly known as Pookoo , is a buddy comedy about a small woodland creature (Jordan) and a majestic bird (Temple) who swap bodies and must team up to survive the wildest adventure of their lives. Nathan Greno ( Tangled ) directs the film from a script by John Whittington, Christian Magalhaes, and Robert Snow, based on a story by Whittington, Adam Karp, Magalhaes & Robert Snow, and Greno. “ Swapped is an unpredictable, emotional ride — full of humor, spectacle, and heart,” said Greno. “We drew from live-action nature documentaries, exploring the complexity of a wild ecosystem to capture something that feels vibrant and deeply human. Michael B. Jordan and Juno Temple brought such warmth and authenticity to the film. Every moment between them feels alive — funny one second, deeply moving the next. Their chemistry lifts the story and gives Swapped its wings.” John Lasseter, David Ellison, Dana Goldberg, and Mary Ellen Bauder Andrews produce. Sam Rockwell plays a man who comes from the future to save humanity from a rogue AI, and it looks as crazy as it sounds. The official teaser trailer for Good Luck, Have Fun, Don\'t Die has been released by Briarcliff Entertainment. Following its debut at Fantastic Fest 2025, the distributor acquired the unconventional sci-fi epic and settled on a February 13 theatrical release. The film stars Sam Rockwell, Haley Lu Richardson, Michael Peña, Zazie Beetz, Asim Chandhry, Tom Taylor, and Juno Temple. As revealed in the Red Band trailer below, Rockwell leads an unlikely group of heroes to save the world from artificial intelligence, which includes battling an army of people under a zombie-like trance. Good Luck, Have Fun, Don\'t Die seems like Verbinski\'s most relevant work yet, while still retaining his unique penchant for fantasy. After his psychological thriller A Cure for Wellness hit theaters in 2016, the acclaimed director took a long break before returning to the director\'s chair for his new dystopian movie. Fortunately, it seems the wait will be worth it, as Good Luck, Have Fun, Don\'t Die looks to be a worthy entry in Verbinski\'s filmography. Check out the film\'s official logline: A man claiming to be from the future takes the patrons of an iconic Los Angeles diner hostage in search of unlikely recruits in a quest to save the world. What Are Reviews Saying About \'Good Luck, Have Fun, Don\'t Die\'? As of this writing, Good Luck, Have Fun, Don\'t Die has a 94% on Rotten Tomatoes based on 16 reviews. It is the highest score of Gore Verbinski\'s career thus far, and while things will fluctuate when it hits theaters nationwide this February, it has a good chance to remain above Rango , which has an 88% on the review aggregate website. Upon its premiere at Fantastic Fest, critics praised the apocalyptic sci-fi film as a "surreal cyberpunk masterwork," per Cinapse , as well as Sam Rockwell\'s charismatic performance as a man determined to save the world from a dystopian future ruled by AI. Of course, not everyone loved what Good Luck, Have Fun, Don\'t Die had to offer, but most concluded that Verbinski was able to elevate a familiar premise and deliver "a dark, timely, and wildly funny satirical time-travel romp" that feels "entirely fresh and new," according to Sean Chandler . The most promising comparison the film has received is to one of the most memorable Best Picture winners in recent Oscar history, per Variety \'s review: "It takes a virtuoso of his caliber to execute on the movie’s intricate Everything Everywhere All at Once-level imagination." Audiences will be able to judge for themselves when the film arrives in theaters on February 13. Published Wed, 12 Nov 2025 17:47:03 -0600 by Jeremy Konrad | Comments Article Summary Good Luck, Have Fun, Don\'t Die marks Gore Verbinski\'s return with a wild, original time travel thriller. Star-studded cast includes Sam Rockwell, Haley Lu Richardson, Michael Peña, Zazie Beetz, and Juno Temple. The film follows a time traveler taking diner hostages on a world-saving quest, blending genres and suspense. Debuted at Fantastic Fest, now hits theaters February 13, promising inventive action and fresh storytelling. Good Luck, Have Fun, Don\'t Die is a new film from director Gore Verbinski , his first since 2016, and boy, is this one a hell of a way to return. Starring Sam Rockwell , Haley Lu Richardson ("The White Lotus," Split ), Michael Peña ( Ant-Man ) , Zazie Beetz ( Joker , Wounds ), Asim Chandhry, Tom Taylor, and Juno Temple ("Fargo," Horns ), the film is about a man who claims to be traveling back in time from the future and taking a diner full of people hostage, trying to recruit people on a quest to save the world. Matthew Robinson wrote the script for the movie. Verbinski is producing the film alongside Robert Kulzer, Erwin Stoff, Oly Obst, and Denise Chamian. The film debuted at Fantastic Fest this past fall and also screened at Beyond Fest. Good Luck, Have Fun, Don\'t Die Is A Fantastic Trailer "This film is wildly original, endlessly entertaining, and unlike anything audiences have seen before," said Briarcliff CEO Tom Ortenberg, who will release the film in theaters. "After seeing it, we immediately knew Briarcliff was the perfect partner to distribute Gore Verbinski\'s first independent, bonkers movie. We couldn\'t be more excited to share his vision with audiences across the country." Credit Briarcliff Entertainment I am so glad that Verbinski is out of movie jail. He was on a huge hot streak with Disney and the Pirates of the Caribbean franchise when The Lone Ranger stalled his career altogether. I remember seeing The Mexican in the theater way back in 2001, and that movie was one of the first where I started to really notice how different filmmakers\' sensibilities showed on screen. He is so good at action set pieces that I hope Good Luck, Have Fun, Don\'t Die has some really cool stuff happening in that diner. It\'s a real bummer because Derek Cianfrance\'s return to the director\'s seat in nearly a decade (his previous film, "The Light Between Oceans," came out in 2016) is quietly one of the best movies of the year. One of those wild true stories pulled right from the headlines, "Roofman" follows Jeffrey Manchester ( Channing Tatum, once again bringing his enduring appeal to the table ), a U.S. Army veteran who quickly becomes known in North Carolina as the Rooftop Robber. As that nickname entails, he breaks into different McDonald\'s locations and other corporate brand namesakes from the roof in the middle of the night and politely ambushes the staff in the morning. After escaping from prison, however, Jeffrey holes up for months inside of a Toys "R" Us. But he can only stay hidden for so long, as his presence starts to have an effect on the Charlotte community. All of the underwhelming marketing material for "Roofman" sold the film as a zany crime comedy with a nostalgic bent when it\'s really a nuanced and achingly sad dramedy about a good person trapped in a cycle of self-destruction. It not only features an excellent turn from Kirsten Dunst as the kind-hearted single mom that Manchester falls for, but also a career-best performance from Tatum (with Ben Mendelsohn, LaKeith Stanfield, Juno Temple, Uzo Aduba, Jimmy O. Yang, Lily Collias, Melonie Diaz, and Peter Dinklage rounding out the ensemble). If you didn\'t see it in theaters, then you\'ll soon be able to digitally purchase "Roofman" on most PVOD platforms (including Prime Video, YouTube, and Fandango at Home) beginning November 11, 2025. Roofman will be made available to buy on most PVOD platforms Davi Russo/Paramount Pictures If you decide to purchase "Roofman" on any of the many PVOD platforms, it will come out to a $24.99 price tag starting out. I wouldn\'t say this is the smartest way on Paramount\'s behalf to recoup the losses from its theatrical disappointment, though. While I\'m sure "Roofman" will be made available to rent within the coming months, it\'s a big commitment for folks to buy the film outright. Likewise, there\'s currently no word on when the movie will hit physical media stands on 4K Ultra HD, Blu-ray, and DVD, but online pre-order listings indicate it will be somewhere down the line. Should you decide to go with the digital pre-order, however, you\'ll also receive over 45 minutes of bonus material. Specifically: Featurette: Based on Actual Events and Terrible Decisions Featurette: Chasing the Ghosts: The Director\'s Methods Featurette: A Good Place to Hide Featurette: Driving Lesson Featurette: Choir Practice Deleted and Alternate Scenes I have to imagine all of these featurettes and deleted scenes will be made available on the Blu-ray copies of "Roofman" as well, whenever that should come out. Considering the film is being distributed by Paramount Pictures, it will likely be released to Paramount+ within the coming months too. I also have no doubt that Cianfrance\'s latest will finally become the hit it deserves to be once it goes through the home media circuit. A teaser for his upcoming film , “Good Luck, Have Fun, Don’t Die,” was released Wednesday, November 12 by Briarcliff Entertainment . In addition, it was announced that the film had been moved back a few weeks, from its initial January 30 release date to February 13, 2026. Sam Rockwell stars as a man claiming to be from the far-flung future Earth that has fallen into apocalypse and ruin. As the movie begins, he holds up a diner in Los Angeles, searching for recruits to help him save the world from devastation. The teaser teases some modern-day cultural commentary, as the apocalypse seems to involve the increasing power of artificial intelligence, as well as an irreverent tone that mixes action with humor. Alongside Rockwell, “Good Luck, Have Fun, Don’t Die” also stars a large ensemble cast that includes Haley Lu Richardson, Michael Peña, Zazie Beetz, Asim Chandhry, Tom Taylor, and Juno Temple. The film was written by Matthew Robinson, who is best known for writing and directing the 2009 rom-com “The Invention of Lying” and also wrote the script for 2019’s “Dora and the Lost City of Gold.” Verbinski produces the film with Robert Kulzer, Erwin Stoff, Oly Obst, and Denise Chamian. Verbinski made his feature directorial debut with “Mouse Hunt,” a 1997 family comedy starring Nathan Lane and Lee Evans. He rose to greater prominence in the early 2000s, when he directed the successful American remake of the iconic Japanese horror film “The Ring,” as well as the first three entries in the wildly popular “Pirates of the Caribbean” film series. In 2011, he was nominated for an Oscar for his acclaimed animated Western film “Rango.” Other films he directed include 2001 rom-com “The Mexican” and 2005 comedy “The Weather Man.” In 2013, he directed a film remake of the popular pulp hero “The Lone Ranger,” which was panned critically and become a box office bomb. His last film was 2016’s “A Cure for Wellness,” a psychological horror starring Dane DeHaan, Jason Isaacs, and Mia Goth. “Good Luck, Have Fun, Don’t Die” made its world premiere at the 2025 Fantastic Fest in Austin, Texas this past September. Briarcliff Entertainment screenshot by Leslie Katz In the new trailer for the movie Good Luck, Have Fun, Don’t Die , a man claiming to be from the future shows up at a Los Angeles diner to deliver a foreboding warning: “All of this goes horribly wrong.” “This,” of course, is the present. But if the disheveled time-traveling man can recruit a team to join him on a one-night quest to save the world from a rogue artificial intelligence, maybe everything will turn out all right. “The revolution begins tonight,” the man proclaims. The sci-fi adventure comedy from Oscar and BAFTA-winning director Gore Verbinski stars Sam Rockwell as the mysterious visitor, clad in a dripping wet cyberpunk-style suit that looks cobbled together from wires, circuit boards, gears, hoses, tubes and other scraps scavenged from a ruined city. “I come from a nightmare apocalypse,” he tells the stunned diner patrons. “This is the height of f***ing fashion.” Glimpses of the future show a shadowy society where people sit amid the urban detritus sealed off in their VR headsets. MORE FOR YOU Good Luck, Have Fun, Don’t Die film arrives in theaters February 13 from Briarcliff Entertainment, pushed back from its original January 30 release date. It had its world premiere at the 2025 Fantastic Fest in Austin in September. Verbinski, who directed Pirates of the Caribbean , The Mexican, The Weather Man and animated film Rango, teamed with The Invention of Lying screenwriter Matthew Robinson for a tale of an AI that does a lot more than spit out surreal images. This is Verbinski’s first film since the 2017 psychological horror film A Cure for Wellness . “So glad Gore Verbinski’s directing again,” YouTuber Anubrato Roy wrote in the comments section of the trailer. “Looks absolutely unhinged, and Sam Rockwell is always a plus.” The film also stars Zazie Beetz, Asim Chandhry, Michael Peña, Haley Lu Richardson, Tom Taylor and Juno Temple of Ted Lasso fame. Forbes Why A ‘Cultural Surgeon’ Secretly Hung AI Art In A National Museum By Leslie Katz As amusing as Good Luck, Have Fun, Don’t Die appears to be , that yet another film portrays AI as a threat to humanity directly reflects current fears surrounding AI that touch on everything from mass job losses to environmental damage and disinformation spread through deepfakes, with irrevocable consequences. Other recent films to confront include 2023’s The Creator , in which artificial intelligence sets off a nuclear detonation in Los Angeles that pits humans against machines. In T.I.M. , a British thriller from the same year, a humanoid AI servant becomes obsessed with one of its owners and turns dangerous. Ben Child As Gore Verbinski’s AI-apocalypse film Good Luck, Have Fun, Don’t Die hurtles towards us, it’s clear from the over-caffeinated trailer that we won’t be getting another ponderous parable about robot souls, digital enlightenment or the hubris of man Tue 18 Nov 2025 05.56 EST Last modified on Tue 18 Nov 2025 06.29 EST Share I t’s easy to forget, given the current glut of robot-uprising doom flicks, that Hollywood has been doing the artificial intelligence thing for decades – long before anything resembling true AI existed in the real world. And now we live in an era in which a chatbot can write a passable sonnet, it is perhaps surprising that there hasn’t been a huge shift in how film-makers approach this particular corner of sci-fi. Gareth Edwards’ The Creator (2023) is essentially the same story about AIs being the newly persecuted underclass as 1962’s The Creation of the Humanoids, except that the former has an $80m VFX budget and robot monks while the latter has community-theatre production values. Moon (2009) and 1968’s 2001: A Space Odyssey are both about the anxiety of being trapped with a soft-voiced machine that knows more than you. Her (2013) is basically Electric Dreams (1984) with fewer synth-pop arpeggios. No one is suggesting Hollywood should start making films about what AI actually does. It seems unlikely that film-goers would flood to multiplexes to catch a three-act tech farce in which a nefarious algorithm admits it can’t answer the hero’s question because it “doesn’t have access to data yet”. But we should at least be getting something that feels like it’s been inspired by recent developments, rather than expensively produced and lavishly recycled takes on stories we’ve all seen before. From the look of its debut trailer , Gore Verbinski’s Good Luck, Have Fun, Don’t Die may not be the bold reinvention of AI cinema we might want, but it is at least gesturing towards something new. This time, the AI in question doesn’t seem hugely interested in saving or destroying mankind; instead it’s acting like a chaotic, reality-bending dungeon master, running humans through a cosmic escape room for reasons that make sense only to itself. Could machines of the future have taken a note from modern day YouTubers who spend all day and night livestreaming their own digital reality? Is this all just a great big laugh at the expense of humanity by a god-like deity? Perhaps this is more about the Deadpoolisation of modern blockbuster cinema, but the sense I get from this trailer is that Hollywood has finally run out of ways to make AI frightening, wise or soulful, and has decided to make it an endlessly glitched-out nonsense engine instead. A jittery man from the future (Sam Rockwell) bursts into a diner to inform a random assortment of strangers that they must help him prevent the AI apocalypse. Suddenly we’re pinballing between spider-legged dollbots, neon-lit dystopian alleyways and what looks like a giant ungulate striding through suburbia, all intercut with quippy one-liners from people who seem to want to narrate their own AI apocalypse in real time. Mystical triangular glyphs are everywhere and set-pieces arrive with the panicked rhythm of a timeline that’s clearly being reloaded every 30 seconds. There’s a definite hint of Everything Everywhere All At Once in the over-caffeinated speed-cutting chaos too, but at least we’re not being handed yet another ponderous parable about robot souls, digital enlightenment or the hubris of man. Verbinski’s film also stars Juno Temple and Haley Lu Richardson and is out in February, when we’ll presumably find out what unholy combination of prompts caused the timeline to glitch this badly in the first place. Jordan and Juno Temple have joined the voice cast of Skydance Animation ’s upcoming animated feature Swapped , which is set to release in 2026. Swapped , formerly known as Pookoo , is a buddy comedy about a small woodland creature (Jordan) and a majestic bird (Temple) who swap bodies and must team up to survive the wildest adventure of their lives. Michael B. Jordan and Juno Temple brought such warmth and authenticity to the film. Every moment between them feels alive — funny one second, deeply moving the next. Their chemistry lifts the story and gives Swapped its wings.” John Lasseter, David Ellison, Dana Goldberg, and Mary Ellen Bauder Andrews produce. Sam Rockwell plays a man who comes from the future to save humanity from a rogue AI, and it looks as crazy as it sounds. The official teaser trailer for Good Luck, Have Fun, Don\'t Die has been released by Briarcliff Entertainment. Following its debut at Fantastic Fest 2025, the distributor acquired the unconventional sci-fi epic and settled on a February 13 theatrical release. The film stars Sam Rockwell, Haley Lu Richardson, Michael Peña, Zazie Beetz, Asim Chandhry, Tom Taylor, and Juno Temple. As revealed in the Red Band trailer below, Rockwell leads an unlikely group of heroes to save the world from artificial intelligence, which includes battling an army of people under a zombie-like trance. Good Luck, Have Fun, Don\'t Die seems like Verbinski\'s most relevant work yet, while still retaining his unique penchant for fantasy. After his psychological thriller A Cure for Wellness hit theaters in 2016, the acclaimed director took a long break before returning to the director\'s chair for his new dystopian movie. Fortunately, it seems the wait will be worth it, as Good Luck, Have Fun, Don\'t Die looks to be a worthy entry in Verbinski\'s filmography. Check out the film\'s official logline: A man claiming to be from the future takes the patrons of an iconic Los Angeles diner hostage in search of unlikely recruits in a quest to save the world. What Are Reviews Saying About \'Good Luck, Have Fun, Don\'t Die\'? As of this writing, Good Luck, Have Fun, Don\'t Die has a 94% on Rotten Tomatoes based on 16 reviews. It is the highest score of Gore Verbinski\'s career thus far, and while things will fluctuate when it hits theaters nationwide this February, it has a good chance to remain above Rango , which has an 88% on the review aggregate website. Upon its premiere at Fantastic Fest, critics praised the apocalyptic sci-fi film as a "surreal cyberpunk masterwork," per Cinapse , as well as Sam Rockwell\'s charismatic performance as a man determined to save the world from a dystopian future ruled by AI. Of course, not everyone loved what Good Luck, Have Fun, Don\'t Die had to offer, but most concluded that Verbinski was able to elevate a familiar premise and deliver "a dark, timely, and wildly funny satirical time-travel romp" that feels "entirely fresh and new," according to Sean Chandler . The most promising comparison the film has received is to one of the most memorable Best Picture winners in recent Oscar history, per Variety \'s review: "It takes a virtuoso of his caliber to execute on the movie’s intricate Everything Everywhere All at Once-level imagination." Audiences will be able to judge for themselves when the film arrives in theaters on February 13. Published Wed, 12 Nov 2025 17:47:03 -0600 by Jeremy Konrad | Comments Article Summary Good Luck, Have Fun, Don\'t Die marks Gore Verbinski\'s return with a wild, original time travel thriller. Star-studded cast includes Sam Rockwell, Haley Lu Richardson, Michael Peña, Zazie Beetz, and Juno Temple. The film follows a time traveler taking diner hostages on a world-saving quest, blending genres and suspense. Debuted at Fantastic Fest, now hits theaters February 13, promising inventive action and fresh storytelling. Good Luck, Have Fun, Don\'t Die is a new film from director Gore Verbinski , his first since 2016, and boy, is this one a hell of a way to return. Starring Sam Rockwell , Haley Lu Richardson ("The White Lotus," Split ), Michael Peña ( Ant-Man ) , Zazie Beetz ( Joker , Wounds ), Asim Chandhry, Tom Taylor, and Juno Temple ("Fargo," Horns ), the film is about a man who claims to be traveling back in time from the future and taking a diner full of people hostage, trying to recruit people on a quest to save the world. Matthew Robinson wrote the script for the movie. Verbinski is producing the film alongside Robert Kulzer, Erwin Stoff, Oly Obst, and Denise Chamian. The film debuted at Fantastic Fest this past fall and also screened at Beyond Fest. Good Luck, Have Fun, Don\'t Die Is A Fantastic Trailer "This film is wildly original, endlessly entertaining, and unlike anything audiences have seen before," said Briarcliff CEO Tom Ortenberg, who will release the film in theaters. "After seeing it, we immediately knew Briarcliff was the perfect partner to distribute Gore Verbinski\'s first independent, bonkers movie. We couldn\'t be more excited to share his vision with audiences across the country." Credit Briarcliff Entertainment I am so glad that Verbinski is out of movie jail. He was on a huge hot streak with Disney and the Pirates of the Caribbean franchise when The Lone Ranger stalled his career altogether. I remember seeing The Mexican in the theater way back in 2001, and that movie was one of the first where I started to really notice how different filmmakers\' sensibilities showed on screen. He is so good at action set pieces that I hope Good Luck, Have Fun, Don\'t Die has some really cool stuff happening in that diner. Sam Rockwell stars as a man claiming to be from the future who takes the patrons of an iconic Los Angeles diner hostage in search of unlikely recruits in a quest to save the world. He explains to the customers he “comes from a future which is totally, completely f— and I’m here to set it right.” In order to save the future, they’ll have to trust a seemingly crazy man. Haley Lu Richardson, Michael Peña, Zazie Beetz, Asim Chandhry, Tom Taylor, and Juno Temple co-star. The project marks Verbinski’s first directorial effort since 2016’s “A Cure for Wellness”. Matthew Robinson penned the script while Verbinski will produce alongside Robert Kulzer, Denise Chamian, Erwin Stoff, and Oly Obst. It\'s a real bummer because Derek Cianfrance\'s return to the director\'s seat in nearly a decade (his previous film, "The Light Between Oceans," came out in 2016) is quietly one of the best movies of the year. One of those wild true stories pulled right from the headlines, "Roofman" follows Jeffrey Manchester ( Channing Tatum, once again bringing his enduring appeal to the table ), a U.S. Army veteran who quickly becomes known in North Carolina as the Rooftop Robber. As that nickname entails, he breaks into different McDonald\'s locations and other corporate brand namesakes from the roof in the middle of the night and politely ambushes the staff in the morning. Briarcliff Entertainment screenshot by Leslie Katz In the new trailer for the movie Good Luck, Have Fun, Don’t Die , a man claiming to be from the future shows up at a Los Angeles diner to deliver a foreboding warning: “All of this goes horribly wrong.” “This,” of course, is the present. But if the disheveled time-traveling man can recruit a team to join him on a one-night quest to save the world from a rogue artificial intelligence, maybe everything will turn out all right. “The revolution begins tonight,” the man proclaims. The sci-fi adventure comedy from Oscar and BAFTA-winning director Gore Verbinski stars Sam Rockwell as the mysterious visitor, clad in a dripping wet cyberpunk-style suit that looks cobbled together from wires, circuit boards, gears, hoses, tubes and other scraps scavenged from a ruined city. “I come from a nightmare apocalypse,” he tells the stunned diner patrons. “This is the height of f***ing fashion.” Glimpses of the future show a shadowy society where people sit amid the urban detritus sealed off in their VR headsets. MORE FOR YOU Good Luck, Have Fun, Don’t Die film arrives in theaters February 13 from Briarcliff Entertainment, pushed back from its original January 30 release date. It had its world premiere at the 2025 Fantastic Fest in Austin in September. Verbinski, who directed Pirates of the Caribbean , The Mexican, The Weather Man and animated film Rango, teamed with The Invention of Lying screenwriter Matthew Robinson for a tale of an AI that does a lot more than spit out surreal images. This is Verbinski’s first film since the 2017 psychological horror film A Cure for Wellness . “So glad Gore Verbinski’s directing again,” YouTuber Anubrato Roy wrote in the comments section of the trailer. “Looks absolutely unhinged, and Sam Rockwell is always a plus.” The film also stars Zazie Beetz, Asim Chandhry, Michael Peña, Haley Lu Richardson, Tom Taylor and Juno Temple of Ted Lasso fame. Forbes Why A ‘Cultural Surgeon’ Secretly Hung AI Art In A National Museum By Leslie Katz As amusing as Good Luck, Have Fun, Don’t Die appears to be , that yet another film portrays AI as a threat to humanity directly reflects current fears surrounding AI that touch on everything from mass job losses to environmental damage and disinformation spread through deepfakes, with irrevocable consequences. Other recent films to confront include 2023’s The Creator , in which artificial intelligence sets off a nuclear detonation in Los Angeles that pits humans against machines. In T.I.M. , a British thriller from the same year, a humanoid AI servant becomes obsessed with one of its owners and turns dangerous.
